items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Lamar or Limmie as some people called him was not a heavy drinker, but Lyman after we finished our work at 3 in the morning, would go to a bar... He and Lamar had their bottles and a glass on the bandstand quite often.

ctx.x: A real genius, which he was. From that night on, Smittie began to call me "Mighty" and I suppose it was because he appreciated the fact that I had been fortunate enough and capable of recording with such a great musician as Django.

George Duvivier and Smittie had been friends for many years and Smittie told me that he was the first one to give George lessons in harmony. George was not a drinking person, so he did not have the same thing there in common as did Smittie and I. And speaking of drinking, Lyman Vunk could drink us all under the table and walk a straight line from Central Park to Times Square. He and Lamar had their bottles and a glass on the bandstand quite often. Lamar or Limmie as some people called him was not a heavy drinker,…

We had a show to play twice a night, The first one at 10:30, and the other at 1:30 a.m. There were chorus girls, singers and the usual cabaret routine, but one of the stars was a comedian known as Dusty Fletcher whom I had seen many times. But the act that he did was very funny and sometimes, above the heads of some of the clients, because it was typical Negro comedy, and the Broadway cabaret cliental were mostly well-to-do white people.
